title: Swiss exporters faced very different real exchange rates behind a relatively stable national index
summary: Martin Schlegel’s presentation in St Gallen on 3 November puts Switzerland’s export resilience alongside a sharp rise in the nominal franc. His charts show how both can be true. Differences in prices across countries and industries alter the competitive effect of a currency move. At the same time, a strong contribution from a few export sectors can lift Swiss GDP even when investment and private consumption grow more slowly. The presentation reviews the September monetary assessment and illustrates how the SNB gathered information. It announces no new interest-rate decision.

Real output is indexed to the fourth quarter of 2019. By the end of the Swiss line in slide 3, output had risen by about 14% from that base, ahead of the euro area and behind the US. The successive panels on slides 4–6 show Swiss exports at about 125 on the index, with consumption and investment below 110. These are levels relative to the same base. Calculating each component’s contribution in percentage points to GDP growth would also require expenditure weights and imports. Export-sector growth in slide 7 is a separate, nominal comparison. Pharmaceuticals and chemicals grew around 30% from the base, watches around 25%, while machinery was slightly below its starting level. A manufacturer’s operating environment could therefore look much weaker than the aggregate trade figures.

The distinction between nominal and real currency exposure is particularly striking. Slides 8 and 9 start both effective exchange-rate indices at 100 in January 2020. By the end of the comparison, the trade-weighted nominal franc ends near 125. Its real counterpart finishes much closer to 100, after moving up and down over the period. Even this adjusted average obscures different exposures. Slide 10’s sectoral comparison against the euro from January 2020 to August 2026, based mainly on producer prices, shows real appreciation of roughly 12% for electronics and optics including watches, versus a real depreciation of around 9% for pharmaceuticals. Tourism uses consumer prices. Separate currency-area contributions also varied over time. The charts do not establish how much any particular exporter passed through to its customer or absorbed in its margin.

The SNB’s regional interviews provide a different window on activity. Slide 13 uses responses through 8 September 2026. In those interviews, the expected change in real turnover over the next two quarters had picked up again. These are companies’ expectations recorded in conversations. They complement the observed national accounts and cannot establish that demand later materialised. The 24 September forecast allowed for annual GDP growth of 1.5–2% in 2026 after an unusually strong second quarter, with a more moderate pace expected over the following quarters. Schlegel’s 3 November presentation retains that forecast vintage.

Oil products accounted for most of the increase in Swiss inflation between February and September 2026. Energy’s contribution was about eight tenths of a percentage point on the chart, while several other categories made small or negative contributions. Slide 16’s September conditional inflation forecast sits above June’s for much of the near horizon, with a smaller difference further out. Both projections assume a policy rate of 0%. The September annual averages displayed are 0.7% in 2026 and 0.8% in both 2027 and 2028. Interpreting the higher near-term profile requires attention to the energy contribution and the common rate assumption. No traded path or expected subsequent rate vote is shown.

questions.question: How much of the nominal franc move was absorbed by exporters’ margins?
questions.detail: The industry-specific real exchange rates show relative producer-price developments, not profit per unit. To evaluate an exporter, compare selling prices, invoicing currencies, imported-input costs and the currency of its production base, separating translation of foreign revenues from a change in pricing power. Equal bilateral nominal exposure could generate very different earnings outcomes across the industries in slide 10.

questions.question: Will recent export strength carry through to domestic investment and demand?
questions.detail: The export volume index rose faster than investment or consumption, and the sector chart shows pronounced concentration. Check disaggregated export volumes, new orders, orders for Swiss machinery and the following regional interviews. Stronger turnover expectations followed by broadening realised domestic activity would support a different growth inference from another pharmaceutical-led increase accompanied by weak capital spending.

questions.question: What would turn the energy-driven increase into a more persistent policy problem?
questions.detail: The price contribution covers February to September, and the conditional projection assumes a constant rate. Compare subsequent domestic services inflation, firms’ selling-price intentions and the next forecast produced on a comparable policy assumption. Additional broad price increases would change the policy interpretation more than another revision limited to oil products. The presentation gives neither market expectations nor a response coefficient.
